faq.q: How does a hydrofoil make lift?
faq.a: The foil is shaped and angled like a wing. As water flows over it, the foil turns the flow downward and the pressure above it drops, giving an upward lift force.
asks: Is a hydrofoil like a wing?

faq.q: Why does the hull rise out of the water?
faq.a: Lift grows with speed. Once the foils make lift equal to the boat's weight, the hull is pushed up clear of the water.
asks: When does a hydrofoil take off?

faq.a: A propeller or water jet on the struts, or sails on a racing yacht, provide the thrust. With the hull clear of the water, much less thrust is needed for high speed.

faq.q: Why is a hydrofoil faster than a normal boat?
faq.a: A normal hull has to push lots of water aside and makes big waves, which causes large drag. Up on its foils, only small foils and struts are in the water, so drag is much lower.
asks: Why does lifting out of the water reduce drag?

faq.q: Why does a hydrofoil sink back down at low speed?
faq.a: Lift depends on speed. When the boat slows, the foils make less lift than its weight, so the hull settles back into the water.
asks: What happens when a hydrofoil slows down?

facts: Water is about 800 times denser than air, so small foils can lift a heavy boat.
America's Cup racing yachts fly on hydrofoils and can sail faster than the wind.
Hydrofoil ferries have carried passengers on rivers, lakes and seas since the mid-twentieth century.
